Blood tests like RF and anti-CCP are widely used to support a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis because many patients test positive, but they are not definitive on their own [d1,d2,d3,d5]. Around 20–40% of people with RA are seronegative and lack these antibodies, which complicates diagnosis based solely on bloodwork [d4,d7,d8]. Authoritative sources explicitly caution that a single blood test cannot confirm RA; diagnosis relies on combining clinical evaluation, symptoms, and imaging alongside blood markers [d4,d8,d9,d10]. Because some sources imply blood tests can “help confirm” RA while others state they cannot diagnose RA alone, there is a genuine disagreement in emphasis and interpretation of the evidence [d1,d2,d3,d5,d8,d9,d10].
